title: CVIP: Comprehensive Vessel Inspection Programme for Ship Owners
description: CVIP, the Atlantis Comprehensive Vessel Inspection Programme: a baseline and repeat inspections of hull, tanks, piping and machinery, with one trend record.
h1: CVIP: One Comprehensive Vessel Inspection Programme for the Whole Ship
intro: CVIP, the Comprehensive Vessel Inspection Programme, is an Atlantis NDT programme for ship owners and managers; it is not an IMO, flag or classification society scheme. It brings together inspections an owner usually buys one at a time, from thickness gauging and crack detection to piping, hatch covers, coatings, thermography, vibration and noise, into one plan for the ship: a baseline visit, repeat visits timed to the survey cycle and port calls, one report format and one trend record for as long as the programme runs.

highlights.h: One plan instead of six contractors
highlights.p: Gauging at the docking, thermography from one firm, vibration from a maker's engineer, hatch tests from another: each report has its own format and its own points. CVIP puts every inspection on one plan, one set of marked locations and one report the technical manager can read in a sitting.

highlights.h: Timed to surveys and port calls
highlights.p: Repeat visits are scheduled against the class survey dates, the next docking and the ports the ship actually uses, so the readings arrive when they can still change a decision: before the steel list is written, before a charter starts, before a sale is negotiated.

highlights.h: A record that stays with the ship
highlights.p: Every visit adds to the same trend record, which the owner keeps. Charterers' vetting questions, a lender's technical review and a buyer's inspection can all be answered from measured history rather than from the condition on one afternoon.

sections.h: What CVIP is, and what it is not
p: Most ships are inspected in fragments. Thickness measurement happens when a survey forces it, crack detection when a crack is already suspected, thermography when an insurer asks, vibration readings when a pump starts to complain. Each job is done well enough, but the reports use different formats, the measurement points move from one contractor to the next, and nobody can say whether the ship is getting better or worse. CVIP replaces those fragments with one programme planned around the ship's structure, systems and trade.

It sits beside the statutory and class framework, not inside it. CVIP does not replace annual, intermediate or renewal surveys, the Enhanced Survey Programme for tankers and bulk carriers, the IMO Condition Assessment Scheme or a class Condition Assessment Programme, and it does not produce a rating. It produces measured evidence that belongs to the owner. The programme draws on these individual services, each described on its own page:

p: The owner chooses the modules; most programmes take all of the first six and add noise where accommodation or crew complaints make it relevant. Timings below are the usual pattern and are fixed for each ship in the programme plan.

p: The baseline decides how useful every later visit will be, so it is planned from the ship's documents before the team travels: structural drawings with original scantlings, the last thickness measurement report, the class survey status and any outstanding conditions, the equipment register from the planned maintenance system, earlier thermal or vibration reports, and the noise survey report. From those, and from the known weak points of the ship type, we draw up the inspection plan with the technical manager: which tanks and holds to enter, where to place thickness and crack detection points, which machines to measure and in what operating condition.

On board, every location is numbered, marked and photographed, and machinery readings are taken with the load recorded. The baseline report describes the ship as found, flags anything that needs action now, and fixes the reference against which every later visit is compared. On an older ship it is often the first time the owner has seen hull, piping and machinery condition in one document.

sections.h: Repeat visits timed to the survey cycle and port calls
p: After the baseline, visits are laid out against the ship's own calendar. A visit some months before an intermediate or renewal survey shows what the surveyor is likely to find while there is time to act. A pre-docking round gives the yard a steel and pipe renewal list before it writes its estimate, and a short visit after the docking re-baselines the items that were repaired. Between those, machinery and corrosion hot spots are checked at the intervals their trends call for.

Teams are mobilised from India for each visit, so visits are tied to ports the ship uses regularly where possible, and to stays long enough for tanks to be gas-freed and released or machinery to be run at load. When a trade changes or a docking moves, the programme moves with it; the plan is a working document, not a contract schedule that ignores the ship.

sections.h: One report format and one trend record
p: Every visit produces the same report structure, so a superintendent who has read one can read them all. It opens with the condition of each area and system, then the changes since the last visit and since the baseline, then the defects and findings ranked by priority with a recommended action and a suggested time to act, usually before the next voyage, before the next survey or at the next docking. Photographs, sketches, readings and calibration records follow.

Behind the report sits the trend record: every thickness point with its history and corrosion rate, every machine with its vibration trend, every thermal finding with its temperature rise over time. The record is delivered as data files the owner keeps, in a form that can be loaded into the planned maintenance system or handed to a future manager, charterer, lender or buyer.

sections.h: What the owner gets from the programme
p: The return on a programme is measured in decisions made earlier and with better information. The points below are what owners usually set out to achieve when they start one.
list: Fewer surprises at the special survey: wastage and cracking are found and planned for before the surveyor and the yard find them
Earlier steel and repair planning, with renewal lists that the yard can work from and parts ordered before the ship arrives
Evidence for charterers and vetting inspectors that the hull, closing appliances and machinery are maintained by measurement, not by age alone
Technical history a lender can review when financing or refinancing the ship
A clean, consistent record when the ship is sold, which shortens the buyer's own inspection and narrows what is left to argue about
Machinery faults caught as trends, reducing breakdowns at sea and the off-hire that follows them

p: Sister ships share drawings, structural details and machinery, and usually share weaknesses. In a fleet programme the measurement plan is laid out once for the class of ship, with the same point numbering on each hull, so readings can be compared ship against ship as well as visit against visit. A crack at a hatch corner on one ship, or a bearing frequency rising on a sister's ballast pump, tells us exactly where to look first on the others.

Fleet results are also reported side by side, which helps a technical department decide which ship goes to the yard first, which needs steel work at its next docking, and which can safely run on. Each ship still receives its own report and keeps its own trend record for the day it changes hands.

sections.h: Where CVIP sits beside class, and who does the work
p: Thickness measurement credited to a class survey has to be carried out by a firm approved by the ship's classification society under IACS UR Z17, with the society's surveyor attending as its rules require. Atlantis is in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS. Until a certificate is issued, CVIP readings serve the owner's own decisions: steel and docking planning, checks between surveys, evidence for charterers and financiers, and the ship's record for a future sale. Ultrasonic tightness testing of hatch covers for class purposes follows the same rule, so in CVIP it is the owner's check.

Each programme is planned and supervised by the founder, our Responsible NDT Level III, who holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT and has more than eleven years of international field experience. Technicians are qualified and certified under our written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and vibration and thermography are carried out by qualified analysts and thermographers to written procedures. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If a class rule, a yard or a charterer requires a particular certification scheme for NDT operators, tell us at enquiry and we confirm before anything is booked.

faqs.q: Is CVIP a class or IMO scheme?
faqs.a: No. CVIP is a programme Atlantis NDT offers to ship owners and managers, and it is commissioned and owned by them. It does not replace any class survey, the Enhanced Survey Programme, the IMO Condition Assessment Scheme or a class Condition Assessment Programme, and it does not award a rating. Its value is the measured, repeatable record it builds, which the owner can show to charterers, lenders and buyers.

faqs.q: Can CVIP thickness readings be used for a class survey?
faqs.a: Readings credited to a class survey must be taken by a firm approved by the ship's classification society under IACS UR Z17. Atlantis is in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS, and until a certificate is issued CVIP readings serve the owner's decisions. Many owners use the pre-docking CVIP round to size the steel work, then have the class-credited gauging done during the survey itself.

faqs.q: How long does a programme run?
faqs.a: Most owners set it up for at least one survey cycle, from one renewal survey to the next, because that is the period over which trends become decisive. It can start at any point in the cycle; starting a year or two before a renewal survey is common, since the first findings then feed straight into the docking. Fleet programmes usually run for as long as the ships stay in the fleet.

faqs.q: What does the owner need to provide for the baseline?
faqs.a: Structural drawings with original scantlings, the last thickness measurement report, the class survey status, the equipment register or planned maintenance codes, earlier thermography, vibration and noise reports if any, the trading pattern and the next docking date. On board, the ship provides gas-free certificates and entry permits for tanks and holds, lighting and access, and engineers to run machinery at the agreed load.

faqs.q: Can we start with one ship and add sisters later?
faqs.a: Yes. The first ship's plan is laid out so it can be repeated: point numbering follows the structure and the equipment register, not one hull. When a sister joins, she gets the same plan and her baseline can be compared directly with the first ship's history. That comparison is often the quickest way to find which ship in a class is ageing fastest and why.

faqs.q: Does a CVIP record help when the ship is sold?
faqs.a: It usually helps both sides. The seller can show a consistent history of thickness, crack detection and machinery readings instead of a single recent report, and the buyer's own Pre-Purchase Inspection can concentrate on checking that history rather than starting from nothing. The buyer still decides what to inspect and obtains the class records through the society with the seller's consent; the CVIP record supports that work rather than replacing it.
